# Generated files: the contributor contract

GitFactory compiles blueprints into real files — most visibly GitHub Actions
workflows. Those compiled files live in the repository alongside hand-written
code, which makes them easy to mistake for something you can just edit.

You can't. This page explains why, and what to do instead.

---

## TL;DR

1. If a file has a **`GENERATED BY GITFACTORY`** header, **do not hand-edit it.**
2. Every generated file is **owned by a blueprint** under `.factory/`.
3. Change the blueprint, then **regenerate**.
4. Commit the regenerated output **in the same PR** as the blueprint change.

A CI check enforces rule 4 by recompiling and failing if the result differs from
what's committed. If that check is red, jump to
[The staleness check failed](#the-staleness-check-failed).

---

## 1. How to recognise a generated file

Generated files carry a header banner near the top containing the string
`GENERATED BY GITFACTORY`. In YAML it appears as a comment block; the exact
wording also names the owning blueprint.

To list every generated file in a checkout:

```bash
grep -rl "GENERATED BY GITFACTORY" . --exclude-dir=node_modules --exclude-dir=.git
```

Run that before you start editing anything under `.github/workflows/` — it is the
fastest way to find out whether the file in front of you is source or output.

> **If a file has the header and you edit it anyway:** your edit survives until
> the next compile, then vanishes silently. That is the failure mode this whole
> contract exists to prevent. It is not a lint preference; it is data loss.

---

## 2. Who owns what

The blueprints under `.factory/` are the source of truth. Each one compiles to
one or more output files, and no output file has more than one owner.

<!-- TODO(maintainer): fill this table in from the actual contents of .factory/.
     One row per blueprint. The generated header in each output file should name
     its owner, so `grep -r "GENERATED BY GITFACTORY" -A2` is a good way to
     derive this table mechanically. -->

| Blueprint (source) | Generates (output) |
| --- | --- |
| `.factory/<blueprint>.<ext>` | `.github/workflows/<workflow>.yml` |

If you can't tell which blueprint owns a file, read the file's own header — it
names its owner. If the header doesn't name one, that's a bug in the compiler
worth reporting.

**Adding a new automation?** Add or edit a blueprint in `.factory/`. Do not
hand-write a workflow YAML — a hand-written file with no owning blueprint will
either be clobbered or drift out of the system entirely.

```bash

```

Context for whoever fills that in — the following are documented in the
[README](../README.md) and are the only compile-adjacent entry points confirmed
so far:

- **The canvas UI.** `cd app && npm install && npm run dev`, then press
  **Compile** to see the generated workflows.
- **The Claude Code command** `/compile-check`, available from `.claude/commands/`.
- **Docker, if you'd rather not install Node locally:**

  ```bash
  docker compose up dev                        # dev server + HMR → http://localhost:5173
  docker compose run --rm dev npm test         # run the vitest suite
  docker compose run --rm dev npm run build    # produce app/dist
  ```

After regenerating, check what moved:

```bash
git status
git diff
```

The diff should contain only your intended change, expressed in the generated
output. Unexpected churn (reordered keys, whitespace, version bumps) usually
means your local compiler version differs from CI's — say so in the PR rather
than committing the noise.

---

## 4. Commit the output with the blueprint

Blueprint and generated output go in the **same commit**, or at minimum the same
pull request. Never one without the other.

Why this matters:

- **The emitted YAML has to work without GitFactory existing.** That is a stated
  design goal of the project. A repo whose workflows lag behind its blueprints
  is running automation nobody reviewed.
- **Review happens on the output.** The blueprint says what you meant; the
  generated workflow says what will actually run in CI with your credentials.
  Reviewers need both to reason about a change.
- **`git blame` stays honest.** A split PR makes the generated file look like it
  changed for no reason.

A correct PR touching automation looks like:

```
modified:   .factory/<blueprint>.<ext>          ← what you edited
modified:   .github/workflows/<workflow>.yml    ← what the compiler produced
```

---

## The staleness check failed

CI recompiles the blueprints and compares the result against what's committed.
A red check means those two disagree. In order of likelihood:

**1. You edited a generated file by hand.**
Revert it, make the equivalent change in the owning blueprint, regenerate:

```bash
git checkout -- <the/generated/file>
# edit the owning blueprint under .factory/ instead, then regenerate
```

**2. You edited a blueprint but forgot to regenerate.**
Regenerate, then commit the result:

```bash
# regenerate (see section 3)
git add -A
git commit -m "chore: regenerate workflows"
```

**3. You changed the compiler itself.**
A compiler change usually rewrites *every* generated file. That's expected — but
keep it in its own PR where possible, so the large mechanical diff doesn't hide
a behavioural change. Regenerate everything and commit it.

**4. Someone else's merge left the tree stale.**
Rebase on the default branch, regenerate, and mention it in the PR so the fix
isn't attributed to your change.

If none of these apply, the check itself may be wrong. Open an issue rather than
editing a generated file to make CI green — a green check bought that way is a
lie the next contributor inherits.

---

## Exceptions

There are none. If a generated file needs a shape the compiler can't produce,
that's a gap in the compiler or the blueprint schema (see `schema/`), and fixing
it there benefits everyone. Hand-patching the output helps exactly one person,
once, until the next compile.
